sekai.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, past the vending machine that shouldn't be there, the path just stops — worn smooth by one <kanji>generation</kanji> of hikers after another — and the whole valley unrolls below: rivers, rooftops, a train crawling through it like a toy. You did not climb to see a view. You climbed to see the entire <kanji>world</kanji> laid out under your boots.
sekai.reading_mnemonic: 世 gives せ and 界 gives かい, combining to <reading>せかい</reading>.

keizai.meaning_mnemonic: In the temple's back room, the loom keeps working: thread after thread <kanji>passes through</kanji> the frame while the monk drones on. What is threaded today is not cloth but coins, spooled from house to market to house again. That endless circuit of coin passing through the village is the economy.
keizai.reading_mnemonic: 経（けい）＋済（ざい）read straight through give <reading>けいざい</reading>, the thread of coin passing through the whole economy.

seiji.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the cats have organized themselves into a council. Every evening they gather on the mossy steps, yowling over who gets the sunniest step, who patrols the gate, who rings the enormous bell at dawn, and only once the vote is cast does the yard finally <kanji>calm down</kanji>. It is petty, procedural, and utterly serious — cats running the shrine until it goes quiet is what <kanji>politics</kanji> looks like.
seiji.reading_mnemonic: 政 gives せい, like Sei, and 治 gives じ, combining to <reading>せいじ</reading>.

iken.meaning_mnemonic: That same eye-on-legs from before does not just wander to <kanji>see</kanji> things — it is opinionated, carrying some stubborn <kanji>idea</kanji> behind its stare. It stops at the school gate, tilts back, and clearly does not approve of the new paint job. It plants itself there until someone stops to hear what it thinks. That stubborn, unsolicited stance is an opinion.
iken.reading_mnemonic: 意 gives い and 見 gives けん, like Ken, combining to <reading>いけん</reading>.

setsumei.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane corners you over the empty offering plate. You stall until dawn's <kanji>bright</kanji> floods both shrine windows at once, sun in one pane, moon still pale in the other, till the courtyard glows so hard the cats squint. In that light your excuse turns readable, laid out plain — an <kanji>explanation</kanji> you never meant to give.
setsumei.reading_mnemonic: 説（せつ）＋明（めい）read straight through give <reading>せつめい</reading>, the explanation laid out plain.

shakai.meaning_mnemonic: Behind the shrine, dozens of <kanji>company</kanji> signposts stand staked in rows, each with its own altar showing off to the neighbors. At dusk every cocoon splits at once, workers stepping out to <kanji>meet</kanji> at the table where chopsticks wait crossed for each — a crowd of companies, meeting as one: society.
shakai.reading_mnemonic: 社 gives you しゃ, 会 gives you かい, and company plus meet chains straight through as <reading>しゃかい</reading>.

bunka.meaning_mnemonic: Every hiker who reaches the vending machine atop the mountain trail leaves something behind: a scrap of <kanji>literature</kanji>, a haiku scratched in the paint, a coin balanced on the ledge. None of it was ever official, but each new scratch is a small <kanji>change</kanji> to the pile, and by year three the machine has its own rules new climbers learn just by watching — that unwritten pile of shared habits is culture.
bunka.reading_mnemonic: 文 gives ぶん, like Mon-Bun, and 化 gives か, like Kaa, combining to <reading>ぶんか</reading>.

dentou.meaning_mnemonic: Every spring the same families haul the same boat to the riverbank and launch it from the exact stone their grandparents used, hand to hand they <kanji>transmit</kanji> the same ritual down the generations, though the current shifted downstream decades ago. Nobody remembers why it has to be that stone, only that it always has been — that refusal to move is tradition.
dentou.reading_mnemonic: 伝 already reads でん and 統 already reads とう; stack them and you get <reading>でんとう</reading>, tradition spelled out by its own kanji readings.

boueki.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini turns into a swap meet: register unplugged, a sign taped over it reading TRADE ONLY. A schoolgirl trades her spare umbrella for someone's manga volume; an old man trades a fish for two rice balls. No money changes hands, only goods, back and forth under the fluorescent lights. That shuffling exchange is trade.
boueki.reading_mnemonic: 貿 reads ぼう and 易 reads えき, combining into <reading>ぼうえき</reading>.

yushutsu.meaning_mnemonic: You're back on the mountain trail, staring up at that doubled peak stacked mountain on mountain that means <kanji>exit, leave</kanji>. Today it's not hikers streaming down it — it's crates, lashed onto that wheeled wagon-boat hull built for <kanji>transport</kanji>, cresting the summit one by one and vanishing down the far side, gone for good. That line leaving over the mountain is export.
yushutsu.reading_mnemonic: 輸 gives ゆ and 出 gives しゅつ, joining into <reading>ゆしゅつ</reading> — sounds like "<reading>you shoot</reading>" the goods off the dock and out of the country.

yunyuu.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, a raft of crates, lashed to that wheeled wagon-boat hull built for <kanji>transport</kanji>, drifts in from the far shore. Each one bumps the bank, tips forward, and ducks its head low exactly like that figure stepping through a doorway to <kanji>enter</kanji>. One by one they dip and climb onto dry land, none of them made anywhere near here. That dripping parade coming ashore is import.
yunyuu.reading_mnemonic: 輸 gives ゆ and 入 gives にゅう, joining into <reading>ゆにゅう</reading> — sounds like "<reading>you, new</reading>" arrivals crossing onto the bank.

zeikin.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the donation box sits atop the mossy steps, and every coin dropped in goes under that same solid roof you know shelters <kanji>gold, money</kanji>. But this roof never stays yours: once a month an attendant hauls the box away and hands a slice to the town office. Money you owned, skimmed before you see it again: tax.
zeikin.reading_mnemonic: 税 gives ぜい and 金 gives きん, combining to <reading>ぜいきん</reading> — sounds like "<reading>zay keen</reading>" on the tax collector's cut.

kakaku.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, exhausted hikers finally reach the vending machine wedged at the very top. They feed it every coin they have, and instead of a drink it spits out one soggy receipt with a single number scrawled on it, fixed in place the same way each cat owns one branch of <kanji>status</kanji>. That number is all anyone at the summit ever talks about afterward: the price.
kakaku.reading_mnemonic: 価 gives か and 格 gives かく, together forming <reading>かかく</reading> — like a clock's double "<reading>cuckoo</reading>" call ringing out the cost.

shijou.meaning_mnemonic: A vendor drags his rig out of the <kanji>city</kanji> — cloth roof snapping, pot lid clanging on every curious nose — and plants it on the exact patch of <kanji>place</kanji> marked by the old stake, right where the sun lands every morning. Others follow, banners rising all around that one staked spot, until the empty ground is wall-to-wall stalls: a market.
shijou.reading_mnemonic: 市 keeps its market reading し and 場 keeps its place reading じょう, so lined up together they simply read <reading>しじょう</reading>.

koujou.meaning_mnemonic: That same staked patch of <kanji>place</kanji> doesn't stay quiet for long. Someone bolts tin walls up around the marker, raising that same steel beam upright as the first mark of <kanji>craft</kanji> on the lot, and wheels in row after row of clattering machines, and by the time the sun swings back over its old spot next morning, the empty ground has vanished under an assembly line: a factory now stands where the stake used to be.
koujou.reading_mnemonic: 工's こう — think Koichi, the konbini king — plus 場's じょう fuse directly into <reading>こうじょう</reading> for factory.

nouka.meaning_mnemonic: Move that same <kanji>house</kanji> — pigeon still skidding off the slick roof, still crash-landing on the outraged pig below — into the middle of a rice field. Whoever drags themselves out at dawn to feed both animals under that one roof, day after day, is the farmer, and the whole roof-and-pig shambles counts as the farmhouse.
nouka.reading_mnemonic: 農's のう leads straight into 家's か — think Kaa, the fire-breathing crow — fusing into <reading>のうか</reading> for farmhouse.

kenri.meaning_mnemonic: At the toll bridge, a stone-faced inspector squats on a stool with a rubber stamp shaped like a fist. He won't discuss it, won't negotiate — no stamp, no crossing. The moment your ticket lands under that stamp, the whole bridge is yours to walk, nobody blinks at you, and you walk off with a clear <kanji>profit</kanji> besides. That stamp is not a favor. It is your right.
kenri.reading_mnemonic: 権 reads けん and 利 reads り, combining straightforwardly into <reading>けんり</reading>.

gimu.meaning_mnemonic: Every dawn, the shrine cat draws bell duty, not by choice but by rotation — just one more <kanji>task</kanji> on the list. It hauls the mallet up the mossy steps, swats the bell once, and slinks back down before anyone notices it was there. It never looks like it wants to, and it never skips a morning. That's obligation: doing the thing whether you feel like it or not.
gimu.reading_mnemonic: 義 reads ぎ and 務 reads む, combining into <reading>ぎむ</reading>.

shinbun-sha.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>new</kanji> spicy man is hauling his fresh-cut tree in when a reporter shoves past to <kanji>hear</kanji> whispers through the gate first. She sprints to the shrine, stakes the earth sign by the altar — a <kanji>company</kanji>, official this morning — and phones the scoop in. New, overheard, incorporated: a newspaper company.
shinbun-sha.reading_mnemonic: 新 keeps its しん, 聞 keeps its ぶん, and 社 keeps its しゃ, so stacked together they simply read 「<reading>しんぶんしゃ</reading>」。

kigyou.meaning_mnemonic: The sheep's roadside <kanji>business</kanji> under the tree starts small — one sign, one stool — but word gets around, and soon it's franchising: other sheep hired, matching signs hung across town, still chewing paperwork at the same unbothered pace. Same ground it started on, just grown big enough to call itself an enterprise.
kigyou.reading_mnemonic: 企 reads き and 業 reads ぎょう, combining into <reading>きぎょう</reading>.

genin.meaning_mnemonic: A heron picks its way across the riverbank, water that starts far off in a quiet <kanji>meadow</kanji>, and taps exactly one pebble loose from the little dam holding back the current. That single pebble rolls, knocks the next, and the whole bank slides into the water in one long crash. Investigators trace it back to that one dislodged pebble: the cause.
genin.reading_mnemonic: 原（げん）＋因（いん）combine directly into <reading>げんいん</reading>.

kekka.meaning_mnemonic: A hiker feeds every last coin into the one vending machine improbably parked at the summit of the mountain trail. The machine groans, shudders, and grinds for a full minute before it finally clatters out — not a drink, just a single crumpled receipt. That sad little slip of paper is the result.
kekka.reading_mnemonic: 結（けっ）＋果（か）combine straight into <reading>けっか</reading>.

oya.meaning_mnemonic: Long after the final whistle blows at Sei's school field, that same straining figure is still wedged in the tree, refusing to climb down until the very last player has gone home — because a <kanji>parent</kanji> doesn't stop watching just because the game is over.
oya.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a stray cat's anxious owner comes bounding up the mossy steps shouting <reading>Oh, ya</reading> every time she spots her cat near the bell, the same worried shout that gives this word its reading, <reading>おや</reading>.

fuufu.meaning_mnemonic: Every morning on the same crowded platform, a <kanji>husband</kanji> and his <kanji>lady</kanji>, complete strangers to everyone else, bow to the arriving train at the exact same instant, same depth, same beat, without ever once looking at each other to check. Commuters who watch it happen twice stop assuming coincidence and start assuming married couple.
fuufu.reading_mnemonic: 夫（ふう）＋婦（ふ）combine straight into <reading>ふうふ</reading>.

shuukan-custom.meaning_mnemonic: That duckling from <kanji>practice</kanji> still can't land one clean flight, but it hasn't missed a single dawn either. Same rock, same launch, same scattered feathers, same untouched bead of milk on the lilypad — every morning, rain or shine. Repetition that rigid stops being practice; it <kanji>becomes</kanji> a habit, a fixed custom now.
shuukan-custom.reading_mnemonic: 習（しゅう）＋慣（かん）read straight through give <reading>しゅうかん</reading>, the fixed daily custom.

kokusai.meaning_mnemonic: The walls that turned land into a whole <kanji>country</kanji> don't stop at one border. Push two enclosures far enough and they meet at the mountain trail's marker, walls flush against walls, one vending machine straddling the seam, selling to hikers from both nations without picking a side. That's international.
kokusai.reading_mnemonic: 国 already reads こく and 際 already reads さい; put them together and you get <reading>こくさい</reading>, international spelled out by its own kanji readings.

seifu.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's cats never asked to run anything, but say who decides which offerings the shrine keeps and everyone points at them — the tabby on the steps, the tom who tolls the bell, the kitten who bats stray coins off the ledge. Nobody elected them, nobody undoes it. That's a <kanji>government</kanji>.
seifu.reading_mnemonic: Sei already carries the せい sound, and 府 gives ふ, so stack them and you get <reading>せいふ</reading>, government spelled out by its own kanji readings.

houritsu.meaning_mnemonic: Everyone in town calls her hoary, sue-happy and ancient — she's taken every neighbor to court twice over, the baker for a crooked loaf, the postman for a bent wheel, herself once by accident. She never loses, because she wrote the rulebook the judge still uses. That rulebook is the <kanji>law</kanji>.
houritsu.reading_mnemonic: 法 already reads ほう and 律 reads りつ; stack them and you get <reading>ほうりつ</reading>, law spelled out by its own kanji readings.

gyogyou.meaning_mnemonic: The sheep's <kanji>business</kanji> never leaves the tree, but it stops being small. Hoof-printed contracts go out to every rowboat on the riverbank, crews hauling nets by the ton on the sheep's word alone. The shade-tree stall becomes an entire fishing industry, sheep still chewing the same paperwork — just for a fleet now.
gyogyou.reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, a fisherman hauls in a net so overloaded he loses his footing and yelps <reading>ぎょぎょう</reading> — twice, sharp — exactly like a sailor shouting <reading>Yo-yo, oh!</reading> as the fishing industry's whole catch crashes onto the dock.

shigen.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a survivalist stranded with nothing, nicknamed She-Gen — short for she generates. Whatever's needed, she makes from scratch: rope from vines, fire from flint, food from traps. People stop asking what she brought and start asking what resources she'll generate next.
shigen.reading_mnemonic: 資 gives its reading し and 源 gives げん, fusing directly into <reading>しげん</reading> for resources.

kankyou.meaning_mnemonic: Split the sound in half: con, like context, and kyo, like Kyoto, a place. Together that's the context of a place — everything surrounding it, not the place itself. That's environment: not the mountain, but the thin air, the switchbacks, and the vending machine humming at the summit.
kankyou.reading_mnemonic: 環 gives its reading かん and 境 gives きょう, fusing directly into <reading>かんきょう</reading> for environment.

mondaiten.meaning_mnemonic: Every Monday at ten — mon dai ten — the same meeting happens: the agenda lists one <kanji>topic</kanji>, and someone circles one line on the whiteboard in red and says this, exactly this, is the <kanji>problem</kanji> point. Not the whole plan, just this one <kanji>spot</kanji> where everything goes wrong. Monday, ten o'clock, one circled line.
mondaiten.reading_mnemonic: 問（もん）＋題（だい）＋点（てん）read straight through to spell out <reading>もんだいてん</reading>.

dansei.meaning_mnemonic: At the edge of the rice field, the <kanji>man</kanji> who's been dragging the plow all day straightens up, wipes his brow, and struts over to the census officer's little folding table by the paddy. The officer takes one look at those plow-dragging arms, stamps the box for his <kanji>sex</kanji> the way Sei always triple-stamps the nature box at school, and checks it without asking a single question: male.
dansei.reading_mnemonic: 男（だん）plus 性（せい）simply combine to give this word's reading, <reading>だんせい</reading>, exactly as the kanji readings predict.
dansei.description: 男性 is the neutral, formal word for “male” — the term you'd see on official forms, medical charts, or in a news report, not something you'd casually call a friend. Everyday speech leans on plainer words for “man” instead.

josei.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, that same kneeling <kanji>woman</kanji> from her kanji story does the wash, one arm sweeping through the current in that graceful pose, the other braced on a rock. A monk from Grandma Kane's shrine passes by, glances at the pose, stamps her card for <kanji>sex</kanji> the way the health-form box always gets triple-stamped, and writes one word in his diary: female.
josei.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a hiker named <reading>Jo</reading> collapses at the summit's lone vending machine, which only takes coins from men. She wheezes, '<reading>Jo, say</reading> please,' until someone tapes a fix over the slot: <reading>じょせい</reading> drink free.
josei.description: 女性 is the neutral, formal word for “female” — used on forms, in medical or professional settings, and in news reporting rather than casual conversation between friends.

seinen.meaning_mnemonic: Right at the foot of the scarecrow — that sun-dried <kanji>year</kanji>-board watching one whole loop of seasons — a tiny sprout pushes up, glowing that impossible <kanji>blue-green</kanji> against the dusk, too fresh to remember a single season the board has watched. Young beside a whole year's watch: that's a youth, a seinen.
seinen.reading_mnemonic: せいねん is just 青 read せい plus 年 read ねん chained straight together, exactly how you already know them, giving you <reading>せいねん</reading>.
seinen.description: 青年 describes a young man roughly in his late teens through twenties. It leans literary or formal — you'll meet it in novels, news reports, and set phrases more than in everyday chat.

shounen.meaning_mnemonic: Perched on the scarecrow's shoulder — that <kanji>year</kanji>-worn board that's stood through one whole loop of seasons — sits the tiny scrap left after someone bit a piece out of small: barely anything, barely <kanji>few</kanji>, up there one single loop of the board's watch. That small, that young: a boy, shounen.
shounen.reading_mnemonic: しょうねん is just 少 read しょう plus 年 read ねん chained straight together, exactly how you already know them, giving you <reading>しょうねん</reading>.
shounen.description: 少年 refers to a boy who is still a child — elementary through junior-high age, not yet a teenager stretching toward adulthood. It's also the word behind “shounen” manga and anime, the genre aimed at that age group.

shoujo.meaning_mnemonic: The kneeling figure — one arm sweeping, one resting low — is how you spot a <kanji>woman</kanji>. Slice a dot from her, the way <kanji>little</kanji> pared itself down to barely anything, and shrink that same graceful kneel down small: little years on her now. What's left kneeling there, barely more than a sliver of woman, is a girl.
shoujo.reading_mnemonic: 少 keeps its しょう reading — the same しょう as tiny showy Sho — and 女 keeps its じょ, so together they give you <reading>しょうじょ</reading> exactly as taught.

koibito.meaning_mnemonic: Two legs mid-stride, carrying nothing else — that's all it takes to be a <kanji>person</kanji>. Put two of them on the same street, circling back to the same doorway again and again until the gap between their reaching hands stops meaning anything. The person who keeps walking that loop back to you, on purpose, is your lover.
koibito.reading_mnemonic: You already have 恋 as こい and 人 softening to びと here, so stacked together they spell out <reading>こいびと</reading> straight from parts you know.
koibito.description: 恋人 means a romantic partner you are dating, not a general term for someone you love — don't reach for it with family or close friends, and it carries a much milder, more ordinary tone than the English word 'lover' often implies.

yuujin.meaning_mnemonic: Two hands reach in from opposite directions and close on each other — no pay, nobody's in charge, just a <kanji>friend</kanji>. Give that handshake two legs and send it into a room where everyone stands straighter and full names get read off cards. A <kanji>friend</kanji> greeted like a <kanji>person</kanji> at a podium, not grabbed by the sleeve at recess, is the formal kind.
yuujin.reading_mnemonic: 友 keeps its ゆう reading, and 人 shows up as Jin's familiar じん, so stacked together they give you <reading>ゆうじん</reading> right from the parts you already know.
yuujin.description: 友人 is the formal, written-register word for friend — the kind used in a news report or a wedding speech — not the word you'd reach for casually with a close buddy in spoken conversation.

nakama.meaning_mnemonic: That sliver of sun trapped in the open gate — the <kanji>interval</kanji> between the swinging doors — never sits there alone for long. Someone else keeps stepping into the same shaft of light, closing the gap just by standing there instead of walking through. The one who keeps showing up to stand in your <kanji>interval</kanji> is your companion.
nakama.reading_mnemonic: 仲 keeps its なか reading and 間 shortens down to a bare ま, so together they give you <reading>なかま</reading> straight from the parts you already know.
nakama.description: 仲間 covers anyone who shares your group or team — teammates, coworkers, even members of a gang — not just people you're personally close to the way 'friend' implies in English; the emphasis is on belonging to the same side, not on affection.

kojin.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the crowd moving as one shuffling mass, every stride in lockstep. Then a single <kanji>person</kanji> peels off — two legs striding their own rhythm, carrying nothing else along with them, matching nobody's pace. Cut loose from the mass like that: one set of legs walking its own line is what individual means.
kojin.reading_mnemonic: 個 keeps its own こ, and 人 supplies the じん you already know, together spelling <reading>こじん</reading>.

aite.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank your reflection keeps up its <kanji>mutual</kanji> mirroring, matching every twitch back at you. This time it lifts a dripping <kanji>hand</kanji>, fingers spread from a wrist, out of the water to shake. Whoever's hand meets yours on the far side of that mirror is exactly what the word names — the other party.
aite.reading_mnemonic: 相's あい reading and 手's て reading sit side by side unchanged, giving you <reading>あいて</reading>.
aite.description: This word rarely maps to one fixed English word — depending on context it can mean an opponent in a competition, a partner in a conversation or relationship, or simply the other side of a deal. Let the situation, not a single gloss, tell you which one fits.

kyaku.meaning_mnemonic: The hiker is still camped at the vending machine, boots off, waiting for tea nobody's bringing. A second hiker trudges up, sees the pack and boots claiming the landing, and steps around rather than start a fight. Unbothered, he's still the <kanji>guest</kanji>, still the <kanji>customer</kanji>, whether the mountain agrees or not.
kyaku.reading_mnemonic: 客 only ever says きゃく, exactly as taught, giving you <reading>きゃく</reading>.

okyakusan.meaning_mnemonic: The self-appointed guest from the mountain trail wanders into Koichi's konbini trailing dust, boots over one shoulder, and Koichi doesn't blink — he bows, pulls the good stool from behind the onigiri shelf, and treats him like royalty. Wrap that same <kanji>guest</kanji> in that much ceremony and you've got a customer addressed with real respect.
okyakusan.reading_mnemonic: The polite お prefix and the familiar さん suffix wrap around 客's own きゃく, spelling out <reading>おきゃくさん</reading>.
okyakusan.description: This is the polite, everyday way to refer to or address a customer or guest — the word shop and restaurant staff use for their patrons, equally natural for a guest visiting someone's home. You would never use it to refer to yourself.

ten-in.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>shop</kanji>'s mouth-doorway swallows another customer, and behind the counter the same shell-reading tortoise clips on a laminated badge-purse lanyard — no free fortunes until it's stamped. Ledger updated, badge visible: the shop's own fortune-teller is now on the clock as its <kanji>employee</kanji>, ringing up onigiri and fortunes alike as the shop clerk.
ten-in.reading_mnemonic: <reading>てんいん</reading> is just 店's てん plus 員's いん stacked together, exactly as taught.

koumuin.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi treats the konbini as <kanji>public</kanji> property, doors open to anyone — so when the town needs its <kanji>tasks</kanji> hauled up the mountain trail, spear on one shoulder, stick raised, arm flexed under the load, he's first in line. At the summit the badge-purse gatekeeper stamps his lanyard: Koichi is now an <kanji>employee</kanji> of everyone's business — a civil servant.
koumuin.reading_mnemonic: <reading>こうむいん</reading> stacks 公's こう, 務's む, and 員's いん in order, exactly as Koichi the konbini king already taught you.

shufu.meaning_mnemonic: Fumi doesn't just sweep Grandma Kane's shrine steps — by dawn she's decided which cats get fed first, when the big bell rings, and who's allowed near the incense, running the whole mossy compound like her own home, corner by corner. Nobody assigned her the shrine; she simply is the <kanji>lady</kanji> of the house — exactly what a housewife is.
shufu.reading_mnemonic: <reading>しゅふ</reading> is simply 主's しゅ plus 婦's ふ, the readings you already know.

gakusha.meaning_mnemonic: That swaddled child parked under the roof of scribbled lessons never leaves the <kanji>study</kanji> habit — decades later it's the same stooped shuffle crossing at dawn, toward the library instead of the crosswalk. The neighborhood still can't name that <kanji>person</kanji>, only recognizes the routine: someone who shows up daily for nothing but study. That routine has a name — scholar.
gakusha.reading_mnemonic: <reading>がくしゃ</reading> is 学's がく plus 者's しゃ, back to back, just as you already learned them.

senmonka.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's shrine keeper turned his own <kanji>house</kanji> into a shrine to one gate, sketching the twin panels for hours, timing the clap that traps the darting cat. Ask him anything else and he blinks; ask about the <kanji>gate</kanji> and he won't stop talking. That single-minded devotion is a specialist.
senmonka.reading_mnemonic: 専門家 is just each kanji's known reading stacked in order — 専 as せん, 門 as もん, 家 as か — giving you <reading>せんもんか</reading> straight down the line.

seinenki.meaning_mnemonic: That same vending machine at the mountain trail summit works on the <kanji>person</kanji> feeding it, not just drinks: put in a coin on your twentieth birthday, and you <kanji>turn into</kanji> someone else, the way the machine folded into a bench. One climb up you're a hiker; by the walk down, the paperwork calls you an adult.
seinenki.reading_mnemonic: 成人 is simply 成 read せい plus 人 read じん side by side, spelling out <reading>せいじん</reading>.
seinenki.description: This names the legal, official threshold of adulthood — the age at which the law starts treating you as a full adult — rather than the everyday sense of simply being grown up. You'll meet it mostly in legal, civic, or ceremonial contexts, not casual talk about someone's age or maturity.

guuzen.meaning_mnemonic: Two customers at Koichi's konbini reach for the same torn-label onigiri at once, both getting the clerk's usual shrug — <kanji>sort of thing</kanji>, probably that kind. Neither planned it, neither knew the other was there; they just wanted the same item off the same shelf, together. That collision, from nowhere, is a coincidence.
guuzen.reading_mnemonic: 偶然 stacks 偶 read ぐう and 然 read ぜん back to back, spelling out <reading>ぐうぜん</reading> exactly as you'd expect.
guuzen.description: 偶然 usually functions as its own adverb, 'by coincidence,' sitting directly in front of a verb with no particle attached, rather than needing a grammatical marker the way many nouns do.

sabishii.meaning_mnemonic: Picture Sei's school five minutes after the final bell — lockers slam shut, footsteps fade down the hallway, and the sports field empties out until it's just you and the last echo bouncing off the walls. Nobody waits around for the sound to answer back. That empty hallway, echoing at nobody, is what lonely feels like.
sabishii.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a heron named Sabi stands alone in the current each evening as the boats head home without her. Passersby murmur 'sob, she—' watching her — the sound of <reading>さびしい</reading>, <reading>sob, she</reading> stares at the water instead. One bird, alone at dusk: lonely.
sabishii.description: 寂しい describes the feeling of loneliness itself, not simply the physical state of being alone — you can feel this in a crowd, and you can be by yourself without feeling it at all.

hazukashii.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the whole gym class watches Sei's shorts split clean down the seam mid-cartwheel. Sei freezes with both arms still overhead, sweatband slipping over one eye, as the room goes dead silent — then the sports field erupts in laughter. That specific horror, every eye in the building aimed straight at you, is embarrassing.
hazukashii.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school festival, a boy named Zooka runs the petting-zoo till. When Sei fumbles for coins, Zooka calls out, 'Has our <reading>zoo cashier</reading> caught you short again?' The crowd giggles, Sei's ears burn — that sting is <reading>はずかしい</reading>.

urayamashii.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till beeps and the very last cream bun — the only one left on the whole shelf — slides into somebody else's bag two customers ahead of you in line. You watch it vanish out the door, coins still in your open palm, staring at the empty hook where it used to hang. That specific hollow ache is envious.
urayamashii.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, another customer waves the last cream bun overhead and croons, '<reading>Oo-rah, ya mushy!</reading>' — teasing you with how soft and fresh it is. That taunting little chant is <reading>うらやましい</reading>, muttered every time someone else gets the good stuff.
urayamashii.description: This is envy without malice — wanting what someone else has, not begrudging them for having it. English envious can carry a bitter edge; this word usually stays wistful instead.

mendokusai.meaning_mnemonic: Back at the riverbank, that same <kanji>mask</kanji> won't stay caught. Every time you wade in and grab it, the current tugs it loose again, snagging on reeds, drifting off, needing you to slog back in all over. Chasing one soggy mask for the fifth time, boots soaked through, is exactly the grinding annoyance of troublesome.
mendokusai.reading_mnemonic: Every week that riverbank mask washes up snagged in the reeds again, and old Ken must wade in to fetch it. '<reading>Mend the dock, I sigh</reading>,' he mutters, hauling his tackle box out again. That worn-out groan is exactly <reading>めんどくさい</reading> — a chore that never stays fixed.
mendokusai.description: Very casual and blunt — something you'd grumble to a friend or mutter to yourself about a chore, not language you'd use with a boss or in polite conversation.

kibishii.meaning_mnemonic: Near the top of the mountain trail, the vending machine takes exact change only — no bills, no rounding up, no exceptions — and a hiker who's climbed for an hour gets turned away for being three yen short. No amount of pleading moves it. That is strict — a rule that will not bend for anybody, ever.
kibishii.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the vending machine's owner is a stone-faced woman hikers nickname '<reading>Kibi, she...</reading>' for never bending the exact-change rule. Say it three times fast and you land on <reading>きびしい</reading> — the sound hikers hiss when she turns them away.
kibishii.description: Describes more than strict people — it also covers harsh weather, tough conditions, and demanding standards, wherever something allows no slack.

yasashii-n4.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a stray cat limps up the mossy steps, hissing, ready to bolt. Grandma Kane doesn't grab for it. She kneels, sets down a sliver of dried fish, and waits, hands open, saying nothing. Minutes later the cat eats straight from her palm. That unhurried patience is the whole word: kind, gentle.
yasashii-n4.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane keeps her voice to a near-whisper as she offers the fish, the sound landing like <reading>yah, sashi</reading> — almost sashimi without its last beat: <reading>やさしい</reading>. The cat's ears drop, and it eats calmly from her open hand.
yasashii-n4.description: やさしい shares its exact sound with a completely unrelated adjective meaning easy or simple (different kanji, different word). Context — a person's disposition versus how hard a task is — is what separates them, not the sound itself.

kowai.meaning_mnemonic: Sei stays late to finish laps alone in the empty gym. One by one, the hallway lights click off on their own, and past the vending machine something drags its feet, slow and deliberate. Sei stops breathing. Every echo in that empty school suddenly sounds aimed straight at her. That cold-sweat freeze is the whole word: scary.
kowai.reading_mnemonic: The footsteps stop right behind Sei, and all she can do is <reading>cower</reading> against the lockers, too frightened to turn around. That instinct to shrink back and hide is exactly the sound of <reading>こわい</reading>: scary.

fukai.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, Ren cannonballs off the rope swing expecting his feet to hit sand in two seconds flat. Four seconds pass. Then six. He's still sinking, arms flailing, sunlight shrinking to a coin far above him, before his toes finally brush the bottom. That long drop with no floor in sight is the whole word: deep.
fukai.reading_mnemonic: Ren's friend Kai jumps in and doesn't surface. Ren cups his hands and yells <reading>Fu... Kai?!</reading> — who, Kai?! — into water that swallows the shout whole: <reading>ふかい</reading>. Kai is fine; the river is just that deep.

asai.meaning_mnemonic: Near the vending machine at the top of the mountain trail, a hiker spots a wide pool and cannonballs in, arms crossed, bracing for a plunge. His palms slap the bottom half a second later, mud smearing up both elbows while his knees are still bent for a dive that never comes. The pool barely reaches his shins: shallow.
asai.reading_mnemonic: Mud-streaked, sitting in ankle-deep water, the hiker lets out a flat <reading>ah, sigh</reading> — exactly the sound of <reading>あさい</reading> — and just pours the puddle out of his boots instead of swimming anywhere.

hosoi-adj.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the last straw left in the box is impossibly narrow, thinner than the beeping wire rack it hangs from. You loop it twice around your finger before the tip even reaches your drink, and it still doesn't touch the ice. That barely-there strand is what thin, slender feels like.
hosoi-adj.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, fisherman Hoshi drags out his rubber <reading>hose</reading> to rinse the day's catch, but years in the sun have worn it paper-thin — one squeeze and it goes flat as a ribbon. He groans, "<reading>ほそい</reading>," mourning how skinny it's become.
hosoi-adj.description: This word covers more than physical width. Japanese also uses it for a thin, faint voice, or slim odds, the way English says a "slender chance" — keep that broader thin/weak sense in mind, not just narrow objects.

futoi-adj.meaning_mnemonic: The ladle-fed X-shaped man from that stew story doesn't stop at one drop tonight. Bowl after bowl gets poured onto his belly until his arms shove out even further and his stomach strains his shirt at the seams. There is no other word for a body gone that <kanji>thick</kanji>, that <kanji>fat</kanji>.
futoi-adj.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, hiker Futoshi stubs his toe on a root and it swells thick as that stew-fed belly from the X-shaped man. He hops toward the summit's vending machine yelling "<reading>foot, oy!</reading>" — that yelp is <reading>ふとい</reading>: thick, fat, swollen.
futoi-adj.description: 太い also describes a deep, booming voice or a bold, nervy personality — someone called 太い isn't always overweight, they might just sound big or act shamelessly confident.

nurui.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the tea you left as an offering sits forgotten past the enormous bell's evening ring. It's neither steaming nor cold, just a flat, tepid puddle the shrine cats sniff once and abandon, unimpressed. That disappointing in-between is lukewarm.
nurui.reading_mnemonic: ぬるい is written entirely in kana, exactly as it's read — there's no reading to derive, just <reading>ぬるい</reading>.
nurui.description: Beyond temperature, ぬるい is common slang for something too soft or lenient — a lax rule, a halfhearted apology, or an opponent who isn't trying hard enough.

kitsui.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, your gym shirt comes back from the wash shrunk two sizes, seams biting into your shoulders on the sports field. The coach notices you wincing and barks at you to keep running anyway, his voice as unforgiving as the collar choking your neck. Between the shirt and the shouting, everything today is tight, harsh.
kitsui.reading_mnemonic: きつい is written entirely in kana, exactly as it's read — there's no reading to derive, just <reading>きつい</reading>.
kitsui.description: きつい also describes anything physically or mentally grueling, like a packed schedule or a brutal workout, not just tight clothing or a harsh tone.

yurui.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the caretaker gave up retying the huge bell's rope years ago. It sags across the mossy steps, a cat dozing in the slack loop like another coil. Tourists yank it hard for luck and get one soft, wobbling clonk — the rope, the latch, the whole afternoon: loose.
yurui.reading_mnemonic: Picture Koichi's new hire at the konbini: a guard named <reading>Yuri</reading>, belt notched three holes too big, trousers sliding every time he bows. Koichi keeps yelling to fix it, but <reading>ゆるい</reading> is simply how Yuri operates — sagging, slack, in no hurry to change.

subarashii.meaning_mnemonic: The last runner crosses the line the instant that shaft of sun lands, steam still curling off the soaked track. The drenched crowd forgets their dripping umbrellas and roars anyway — after all that mud, this sudden <kanji>clear up</kanji> isn't just nice weather, it's wonderful.
subarashii.reading_mnemonic: Sound out each piece and you already have it — 素（す）＋晴（ば）＋ら＋し＋い spells exactly <reading>すばらしい</reading>, nothing hidden.

sugoi.meaning_mnemonic: Overnight the riverbank swells into a churning brown flood, flinging fish onto the road and swallowing someone's bicycle whole. Villagers can't decide whether to grab a camera or grab their neighbors and run — it's the kind of amazing that's also terrible, water too enormous to look away from.
sugoi.reading_mnemonic: No kanji hides underneath this one — <reading>すごい</reading> is written exactly the way it sounds, kana straight through.
sugoi.description: すごい covers more ground than English amazing: the same word fits a breathtaking view and a disaster, so whether it lands as delighted or alarmed depends entirely on what's happening around it.

erai.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, a kid arrives dead last, dragging their pack past the vending machine everyone else already raided. Nobody laughs — the group claps instead, because finishing at all after that climb makes the kid great, an admirable kind of great that has nothing to do with coming first.
erai.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, an old delivery man named <reading>Ray</reading> wades across every dawn with a crate balanced on his head. Grandma Kane watches from the shrine steps and murmurs <reading>えらい</reading> — not to a genius, only to someone who quietly does the hard thing every day.
erai.description: えらい praises effort or character more than raw achievement, and it's usually said downward — a boss to a junior, an adult to a child — so aiming it at someone above you can land as presumptuous rather than respectful.

zurui.meaning_mnemonic: Partway up the mountain trail, a line of hikers waits at the one vending machine, patience gone in the heat. A kid slips to the front, feeds it a washer instead of a coin, and walks off with the last cold drink before anyone can stop him. Every hiker behind him mutters the same complaint: sly, and completely unfair.
zurui.reading_mnemonic: ずるい is pure kana front to back — read exactly as written, 「<reading>ずるい</reading>」, with no kanji hiding behind it to decode.
zurui.description: In casual speech ずるい often works as its own exclamation — kids and friends shout it the way English speakers shout "no fair!", not just describe someone as sly.

kayui.meaning_mnemonic: During warm-ups on Sei's school field, a kid drops into push-up position onto an anthill nobody flagged. Within seconds he's rolling sideways, one arm twisted behind his back scratching a spot he can't reach, refusing to stop the exercise. The coach just blows the whistle again. Itchy doesn't begin to cover it.
kayui.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, Kay wades in barefoot and steps straight into a patch of stinging weed. She scrambles out clawing at one shin, yelping “<reading>kah-you-ee</reading>!” loud enough to send the herons flying. That yelp is the reading itself — <reading>かゆい</reading> — scratched right into the sound of the word.

majime.meaning_mnemonic: The kid who fished the <kanji>mask</kanji> out of the river straps it on for the shrine play, but he won't clown around like the others. He plays it <kanji>true</kanji> — nothing held back, nothing faked. Through the mask's two carved holes, his <kanji>eye</kanji>s never once break their stare. That unfaked, unblinking focus is serious, diligent.
majime.reading_mnemonic: At the school gate, Jimmy's mother catches him skipping homework again and barks the same two words every time: “<reading>Ma, Jimmy</reading>!” Said fast, that scold collapses into the reading itself, <reading>まじめ</reading> — exactly what she wants him to become: serious, diligent.
majime.description: 真面目 is usually praise for hard work, but Japanese speakers also use it teasingly, to call someone a stickler or no fun — closer to English "goody two-shoes" than a plain compliment, depending on tone.

nesshin.meaning_mnemonic: Ever since that wall of <kanji>heat</kanji> rolled out of Koichi's microwave, one regular is back every morning for it, first in line before the shutters even lift, practically vibrating while she waits. She doesn't want the onigiri cold — she wants that exact blast, every day, without fail. That relentless craving is enthusiastic.
nesshin.reading_mnemonic: 熱's ねつ contracts to ねっ before 心's しん, giving 「<reading>ねっしん</reading>」 straight from kanji you already know.

kanzen.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi rings up the <kanji>whole</kanji> onigiri shelf in one beep, sweeping every last rice ball into his basket. He studies the bare metal shelf after: no wrapper, no crumb, nothing left behind. The <kanji>whole</kanji> shelf is gone without a trace — flawless, missing nothing. That is perfect, complete.
kanzen.reading_mnemonic: You already know 完 as かん and 全 as ぜん, so simply chain them together to get <reading>かんぜん</reading>.

anzen.meaning_mnemonic: Rain floods the riverbank, but under her little roof everyone stays <kanji>peaceful</kanji> — the storm can't reach in here. Koichi checks the house room by room until the <kanji>whole</kanji> family is accounted for, every single one tucked inside. Peaceful and entire together: nothing missing, nothing exposed. That's what safe means.
anzen.reading_mnemonic: You already know 安 as あん and 全 as ぜん, so chain them straight together to get <reading>あんぜん</reading>.

juubun.meaning_mnemonic: At the mountain trail's summit, a hiker holds up all ten fingers — a perfect <kanji>ten</kanji> — and feeds it into the lone vending machine. Out drops a rice cake, and the woodcutter's sword remembers its old trick: one clean strike, and the cake leans into two even <kanji>parts</kanji>. Ten fingers, one log split evenly — plenty for two hikers, with rations left to spare. That's sufficient, enough.
juubun.reading_mnemonic: You already know 十 as じゅう and 分 as ぶん, so chain them together to get <reading>じゅうぶん</reading>.

fuan.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the stiff figure still won't budge off the mossy steps — <kanji>negative</kanji>, flat refusal, blocking the bell from ever ringing. Cats slip past toward where it should be <kanji>peaceful</kanji>, but the calm never arrives; every attempt to relax gets shut down cold. Blocked peace, permanent refusal — that itch of never quite settling is what anxious, uneasy feels like.
fuan.reading_mnemonic: You already know 不 as ふ and 安 as あん, so chain them together to get <reading>ふあん</reading>.

kiken.meaning_mnemonic: The mountain trail's ridge narrows to its usual knife-edge, ground so <kanji>precipitous</kanji> that the vending machine at the top might as well be on the moon. Someone tries the crossing anyway, boots skidding on gravel, arms out over drops on both sides. Ground this <kanji>impregnable</kanji> and exposed, with nothing to catch you, is exactly what dangerous means.
kiken.reading_mnemonic: 「きけん」 is just the kanji you already know stacked together — 危（き）plus 険（けん） — so read <reading>きけん</reading> straight off the page.

tekitou.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine festival, a cat streaks across the dart stall and knocks the thrower's arm mid-swing. The dart wobbles off any real aim but still drives dead center into the target, feathers up, point on the mark — <kanji>hit</kanji> and <kanji>appropriate</kanji> whether anyone meant it or not. Skill or luck, it works: appropriate, or just random.
tekitou.reading_mnemonic: 「てきとう」 comes straight from the kanji readings you already have — 適（てき）plus 当（とう） — so <reading>てきとう</reading> is just those two sounds glued together.

shoujiki.meaning_mnemonic: Sei finishes sprinting the sports field, toe planted dead <kanji>correct</kanji> on the chalk line, then jogs down to the riverbank to watch the ferryman. Everything there bends — reeds, ripples, the mooring rope — but his eye never wavers, poling <kanji>straightaway</kanji> across without glancing at the crooked water. Two people who refuse to fudge the line is what honest looks like.
shoujiki.reading_mnemonic: 「しょうじき」 is just 正（しょう）plus 直（じき）, the readings you already learned for Sei's line and the ferryman's straight crossing — say them together and you get <reading>しょうじき</reading>.

wagamama.meaning_mnemonic: A kid parks in front of Koichi's onigiri shelf and refuses to move until the till stops beeping their way — not that salmon one, the other salmon one, no, back to the first. Koichi restocks the shelf three times before the kid looks up. Getting exactly what you want, exactly when you want it, every time: selfish, through and through.
wagamama.reading_mnemonic: This word is written exactly the way it sounds, kana all the way through, so <reading>わがまま</reading> is simply read as spelled — no kanji, no decoding needed.

rippa.meaning_mnemonic: You groan the whole way up the mountain trail, bracing for the usual dented vending machine at the top. Instead it stands gleaming, fully stocked, not a scratch on it, like it was airlifted in that morning. Nothing about this altitude explains a machine this splendid, this fine — but there it is.
rippa.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just 立（りっ）＋派（ぱ）read straight through: 「<reading>りっぱ</reading>」.

muri.meaning_mnemonic: The king rams his spiked crown into the ground for pure <kanji>reason / logic</kanji>, measuring every paddy edge against it — but the village has burned down to the same scorched, empty rectangle that <kanji>nothingness</kanji> always leaves. No paddies, no lines, nothing left to measure. He jams the spike into the ash anyway, still demanding perfectly straight rows out of nothing at all. Unreasonable. Impossible.
muri.reading_mnemonic: The reading is 無（む）＋理（り）read straight through: 「<reading>むり</reading>」.

muda.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, someone piles the counter with rice balls, then drops the whole armful reaching for their wallet — every one skids under the beverage case, unrecoverable. What's left on the counter is the same scorched, empty rectangle that <kanji>nothingness</kanji> leaves behind after the gym fire: money spent, nothing to show for it. Wasteful. Useless.
muda.reading_mnemonic: The reading is 無（む）＋駄（だ）read straight through: 「<reading>むだ</reading>」.

kantan-n4.meaning_mnemonic: Everyone treats Grandma Kane's shrine bell like it needs a whole ritual — bowing twice, clapping, murmuring a wish. But the cats have figured out you can just swat the rope once and the enormous bell rings anyway. One paw, one clang, done. No ceremony required: simple.
kantan-n4.reading_mnemonic: The reading is 簡（かん）＋単（たん）read straight through: 「<reading>かんたん</reading>」.

fukuzatsu.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, an old woman ties one wish thread to the bell rope, then another, then a stray cat drags a third one under the mossy steps, and by dusk the whole rope is a knotted mess nobody can trace from start to end — hopelessly, thoroughly complicated.
fukuzatsu.reading_mnemonic: 複 keeps its plain reading ふく and 雑 keeps ざつ, stacking together exactly as expected into 「<reading>ふくざつ</reading>」.

tokui.meaning_mnemonic: In that same hallway at Sei's school, you get so much practice cracking the heart's iron lid that you can do it on command now — a clean little burst of <kanji>idea</kanji> every single time, no fumbling, no missed sparks. You're good at it, and it shows on your face: chin up, proud, ready for the next one.
tokui.reading_mnemonic: 得 keeps its taught とく reading and 意 keeps い, combining plainly into 「<reading>とくい</reading>」.

nigate.meaning_mnemonic: Back at Koichi's konbini, the same customer who bit into that spoiled onigiri now can't make himself reach for another one — his <kanji>hand</kanji> hovers an inch from the shelf and stalls every time, flinching at the memory of that <kanji>suffering</kanji> under the fluorescent lights. Some things you're just bad at facing twice; this shelf is his weak point now.
nigate.reading_mnemonic: 苦 keeps its taught にが reading and 手 keeps て, joining plainly into 「<reading>にがて</reading>」.

jiyuu.meaning_mnemonic: Once the eye in that cracked mirror at Sei's school finally recognizes <kanji>self</kanji>, it stops needing to stare at anything else. It rolls back out of the bathroom, drifts down the empty hallway, out past the sports field and the gate, answering to nobody — total freedom.
jiyuu.reading_mnemonic: 自 keeps its taught じ reading and 由 gives ゆう, combining directly into 「<reading>じゆう</reading>」.

heiki.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the punishing climb just stops — the ground goes <kanji>flat</kanji> around the vending machine. The steam-spirit <kanji>energy</kanji> that was rising off you in frantic puffs the whole way up stops swirling too; it just hangs there, unbothered. Flat ground, settled spirit — that's calm, unconcerned.
heiki.reading_mnemonic: 平（へい）＋気（き）＝<reading>へいき</reading> — straight from the kanji readings you already know.

zannen.meaning_mnemonic: Passing the shrine gate the next day, the guard's broken halberd is still lying where it fell, shaft cracked. All that <kanji>remains</kanji> is the wreckage — a little reminder of what got wrecked, sitting there so nobody can forget it. Looking at it stings every time. That sinking feeling is regrettable.
zannen.reading_mnemonic: 残（ざん）＋念（ねん）＝<reading>ざんねん</reading> — straight from the kanji readings you already know.
zannen.description: 残念 is very often used on its own as an exclamation — 残念！ — meaning roughly 'too bad!' or 'what a shame,' not only as a descriptive adjective inside a full sentence.

todoku-v.meaning_mnemonic: Same room, same sprawled body nobody expects to move for the doorbell. This time nobody's carrying anything — a gust from the open window just nudges the package across the tatami by itself, inch by inch, until it bumps his outstretched leg on its own. Nothing dragged it there. It simply <kanji>reached</kanji> him. That's arriving.
todoku-v.reading_mnemonic: The package never gets carried the last stretch — it slides itself across the tatami until it stops dead against his <reading>toe</reading>, docking there on its own. Nothing pushed it home; it just <reading>とどく</reading>, arrives, all by itself.

todokeru.meaning_mnemonic: The courier from that story refuses to let it slide the rest of the way — he shoulders the whole package himself, weaves past the onigiri shelf, and doesn't stop until he's set it down directly in the customer's hands. Nobody let this one arrive on its own; he made sure it <kanji>reached</kanji> them. That's delivering it, personally.
todokeru.reading_mnemonic: Koichi's courier won't let the box dock itself — he carries it the last few steps by hand and sets it down himself, making sure he's the one who gets to <reading>dock it</reading> at the counter. That deliberate, hand-carried finish is <reading>とどける</reading>: to deliver, on purpose.

naoru.meaning_mnemonic: Your ankle throbs the whole way down the mountain trail, and by the riverbank it's swollen and furious. You lower it into the water behind the stone wall — the wall that <kanji>calms</kanji> the thrashing current into one flat pool. Your ankle obeys the trick: the throbbing settles, goes still — that stillness is what it means to heal, to recover.
naoru.reading_mnemonic: Nao, the medic who patrols the riverbank, carries a first-aid kit that smells like kitchen roux. She kneels by your ankle, says her own name like a charm, <reading>Nao</reading>, then stirs in a spoonful, <reading>roux</reading>. Say the two fast and you get <reading>なおる</reading>: the ankle stops hurting, healed.

tsutawaru.meaning_mnemonic: The courier's message reaches the enormous bell, and the ring takes over on its own: sound rolls off the bell straight through the shrine, mossy step to mossy step, cat to cat, without anyone touching it again. It just <kanji>transmits</kanji> itself outward until the whole hill has heard it — that is what it means to be conveyed.
tsutawaru.reading_mnemonic: The courier's daughter, Sue, runs messages down from the shrine too, and her catchphrase when she arrives out of breath is <reading>Sue-tah-wah-roo</reading> — her way of saying the news made it through untouched. Shout it after her and you're saying <reading>つたわる</reading>: it got through.

mukaeru.meaning_mnemonic: You step off the train at Sei's school stop on your first day, dreading the walk alone across the sports field. Instead a whole line of upperclassmen is standing at the gate for you, waving you in before you've taken three steps alone. That's the meaning in one scene: someone comes out to welcome you in.
mukaeru.reading_mnemonic: The greeter at Sei's school gate has one running joke: he moos like a cow before calling your name, so it comes out as <reading>moo-kai-eh-rue</reading>. That ridiculous chant is close enough to <reading>むかえる</reading> that you never forget it: someone coming out to welcome you in.

mitsukaru.meaning_mnemonic: The eye that grew legs is still out wandering the world, and one afternoon it rounds a corner and stops dead in front of you. You'd been hiding under Grandma Kane's shrine steps, sure nobody would look there, but the moment those legs plant themselves and the eye finally <kanji>sees</kanji> your face, hiding is over — you have been found.
mitsukaru.reading_mnemonic: A kid named Mitsu hides behind the onigiri shelf at Koichi's konbini, certain the seeker will never check there. The seeker rounds the shelf and shouts her name like a chant, <reading>Mitsu-kah-rew</reading> — the whole sound of <reading>みつかる</reading>: the moment hiding stops working.

kimaru.meaning_mnemonic: Back on the mountain trail, the signpost stands long after the hiker has gone. Rain keeps falling, and the wrong arrow's paint keeps washing away on its own, drop by drop, until only the left one is legible. Nobody is holding the brush anymore — the fork simply <kanji>decides</kanji> itself. It's decided, and no one chose it.
kimaru.reading_mnemonic: Kiki the tree spirit feels it settle deep in the trunk's <reading>key marrow</reading> — a knot shaped like a key, hidden in the grain. The wind confirms it and she giggles: <reading>きまる</reading>. Nobody chose this; it simply became so, all on its own.

kimeru-v.meaning_mnemonic: On the same trail, the hiker doesn't wait for rain. She grips the brush herself and drags three deliberate strokes across the wrong arrow, blotting it out on purpose. She wanted this settled, so she <kanji>decides</kanji> for the trail — nobody else touches the brush. Her choice, made by her own hand.
kimeru-v.reading_mnemonic: Kiki holds up a hand mirror shaped like a <reading>key mirror</reading> and stares herself down, choosing on purpose this time. <reading>きめる</reading>, she declares, and taps the glass twice. Her decision, made deliberately, not left to the wind.

tsuzuku.meaning_mnemonic: The stray thread from the shrine cat's blanket keeps unspooling down the mossy steps by itself, past the marching legs, past the saluting duck, with nobody pulling it. It just keeps going under its own momentum — the thread <kanji>continues</kanji>, on and on, because nothing stops it.
tsuzuku.reading_mnemonic: A keeper named Zuzu chases the runaway thread down the shrine steps, muttering under her breath as she follows: <reading>too-zoo-coo</reading>. The sound lands right on <reading>つづく</reading> — and fittingly, her chase never actually ends, she just keeps going.

tsuzukeru-v.meaning_mnemonic: This time it's the samurai duck himself, not the thread, taking initiative: he grabs the loose end and marches it forward on purpose, refusing to let the line stop under his own feet. He isn't watching it continue — he's the one who <kanji>continues</kanji> it, step after deliberate step, by choice.
tsuzukeru-v.reading_mnemonic: Zuzu returns, but this time she isn't chasing — she's hauling the thread forward herself, calling it her <reading>too-zoo-carry</reading> job. She won't put it down, repeating <reading>つづける</reading> under her breath, keeping herself going on purpose, forever.

fueru-v.meaning_mnemonic: The farmer from the <kanji>increase</kanji> story checks his flooded plots at dawn and finds they have already crept past the signpost with no one wading out to widen them — the mud and water simply spread wider in the night, on their own. Nothing pushed the boundary forward; it just grew there by itself. That is what it means to increase, untouched.
fueru-v.reading_mnemonic: Koichi checks the onigiri shelf and swears it has a <reading>fever</reading> — turn your back for five minutes and the trays have doubled, then tripled, spreading like a fever nobody ordered or restocked. That unasked-for multiplying is exactly <reading>ふえる</reading>: things quietly increasing on their own.

fuyasu.meaning_mnemonic: The same farmer behind <kanji>increase</kanji> grabs a shovel at dawn and drags the signpost forward himself, hauling extra buckets of river water into the plots until the mud spreads past yesterday's marker — sweat on his back, deliberately claiming more ground with his own two hands. Nothing about this happens on its own; he is the one making it increase.
fuyasu.reading_mnemonic: Sei corners the copier at school and mutters '<reading>for us</reading>' every time he hits print, deliberately cranking out more flyers than anyone asked for — twenty becomes forty becomes eighty, stacked on purpose by his own hand. That's <reading>ふやす</reading>: not multiplying by itself, but someone making it increase.

heru-v.meaning_mnemonic: The guard's cup from the <kanji>decrease</kanji> story sits forgotten on the gatepost after the halberd clatters down, and through the day it just evaporates on its own — no mouth waiting below this time, only sun and wind pulling one drop after another into the air until the cup stands dry by dusk. Nobody touched it; it simply decreased.
heru-v.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the cats shed clumps of <reading>hair</reading> across the mossy steps every single day, and by evening whatever pile you swept that morning has quietly thinned to nothing on its own — nobody brushes them, it just happens. That fading pile is <reading>へる</reading>: things dwindling by themselves.

herasu.meaning_mnemonic: That same guard from <kanji>decrease</kanji> gets thirsty on watch and starts deliberately tipping his cup toward his own mouth, gulping it down on purpose drop by drop until nothing is left — he chose every swallow, tilting the cup himself rather than waiting for it to spill or dry. He is the one decreasing it.
herasu.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a hiker chugs bottle after bottle at the vending machine, calling each empty can '<reading>her loss</reading>' as she deliberately drains the six-pack down to two before the climb — she is choosing to thin the load herself. That's <reading>へらす</reading>: someone forcing the shrinkage, not letting it happen.

kowasu.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's cat isn't done causing trouble. Now her grandson wants a turn — he grabs a leftover festival mallet and swings at the cracked bell just to see if he can finish the job himself. Every hit is pure, deliberate <kanji>demolition</kanji>: he means to break that bell, on purpose, until it can't ring again.
kowasu.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a delivery koala waves a lawsuit against the bell for scaring off customers. He slaps a notice on the mossy steps and grunts <reading>koala sues</reading> — the same sound as <reading>こわす</reading> — then smashes the noticeboard himself, just to make his point.

kowareru.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane never touches the bell again after the cat incident, yet the cracked steps keep crumbling anyway — a slow, ongoing <kanji>demolition</kanji> nobody is causing. Moss creeps into the cracks, another step gives way each spring on its own, the shrine breaking itself apart with nobody to blame.
kowareru.reading_mnemonic: Up on the mountain trail, the vending machine gives out mid-sale, lights flickering off with nobody around to blame. A hiker mutters <reading>Cora, we're through</reading> — which lands right on <reading>こわれる</reading> — as it keeps dying quietly, no one having touched it.

sodateru.meaning_mnemonic: On Sei's sports field, the groundskeeper isn't satisfied just watering that droopy sunflower — he measures its height every Monday and stakes the stem before storms. He's not letting it fend for itself; he's deliberately <kanji>bring up</kanji>ing it, staking his own reputation on raising one seedling past the goalposts.
sodateru.reading_mnemonic: Every recess, the groundskeeper hands his assistant a can and yells <reading>soda, Teru</reading> — it sounds like <reading>そだてる</reading> — because watering that stubborn sunflower is Teru's whole job now, one fizzy can at a time, until it stands taller than the goalposts.

sodatsu.meaning_mnemonic: Over summer break, the gates to Sei's sports field stay locked and nobody waters the sunflower at all — no groundskeeper, no stake, nothing. Yet it's still there in September, taller than the goalposts, leaves like small hands reaching skyward: it managed to <kanji>grow up</kanji> entirely on its own, no help required.
sodatsu.reading_mnemonic: Weeks later, nobody's watering the sunflower on Sei's field, and it doesn't care — it keeps climbing on its own. A kid passing by shrugs, cracks open a can, and mutters <reading>soda, too</reading>, exactly how <reading>そだつ</reading> sounds, as the plant grows two more inches unattended.

mawaru.meaning_mnemonic: That <kanji>round</kanji> kanji is a mouth boxed in an enclosure, repeating itself. Make the enclosure a revolving door. The mouth rides it and says the same greeting each time it swings past you. The door never stops. It keeps carrying the mouth around to the same spot, again and again. Something that loops back on itself like that is turning, going around.
mawaru.reading_mnemonic: A robot lawn <reading>mower</reading> on the school sports field throws a wheel and spins where it stands. A bored crow hops on for the ride. Round and round it goes, carving one circle into the grass over and over. That helpless, self-driven spinning is <reading>まわる</reading>.

mawasu.meaning_mnemonic: Take that <kanji>round</kanji> kanji as a mouth sealed in a small enclosure. Now it is a hand-crank music box. You grip the handle and turn it. Every full turn you drive drags the trapped mouth through its one tinny song again. Nothing in the box moves unless your hand moves it. You are the one making it go around.
mawasu.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, an old well has a hand winch with a soggy <reading>walrus</reading> draped over the bucket. You crank the handle to haul it up. Every turn of your wrist lifts the grumbling walrus higher. You keep cranking until it flops over the rim. Driving a handle round by hand is <reading>まわす</reading>.

hikkosu.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>pull</kanji> kanji is you hauling a bowstring back with a hooked stick until the bow bends double. Tie that string to your whole apartment — futon, fridge, every box, piled on one groaning sled. Set your heels and haul. The household lurches off down the road to a new address. Dragging your entire home somewhere new is what it means to move.
hikkosu.reading_mnemonic: Regular reading: 引 lends its ひ, the small っ doubles the consonant that follows, and the last kanji with its tail reads straight, giving <reading>ひっこす</reading>.
hikkosu.description: This verb is only for changing where you live. Moving an object across a room, or being moved by a story, needs a different verb.

kayou.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>traffic</kanji> kanji is a walled path that funnels onto one open road where everyone ends up. Put yourself on that road at dawn, then again at dusk, then at dawn once more. Same path, same road, out and back, every day of the week. Wearing a single route smooth by travelling it over and over is to commute.
kayou.reading_mnemonic: A scruffy <reading>coyote</reading> has adopted the lone vending machine atop the mountain trail. Each morning it trudges up the steep path, buys one hot can, and pads back down. Next dawn, up it goes again. Same trail, same machine, day after day. That daily out-and-back trek is <reading>かよう</reading>.

waku.meaning_mnemonic: A battered wok of river water sits on the mossy shrine steps. No stove under it, no flame, nobody watching. By midday the water is rolling and hissing, coming to a full boil all by itself. The shrine cats keep their distance. Nobody boiled this water. It simply boils.
waku.reading_mnemonic: Waku is a cook who owns one <reading>wok</reading> and guards it like treasure. He sets it among the shrine cats, fills it from the river, and lights nothing. The water comes to a boil on its own, right on cue. As it bubbles over he says <reading>わく</reading> to mean it boiled itself.
waku.description: English 'boil' covers both the water boiling and a person boiling it; Japanese keeps them apart. This is the intransitive side: the water or bath comes to a boil by itself, as the subject. A person boiling something takes a separate transitive verb.

wakasu.meaning_mnemonic: A tour guide barges into the konbini, past the onigiri shelf, promising to 'walk us straight to a boil.' He drops a huge pot on the beeping till, cranks the burner high, and stirs until the water boils. Someone always does the boiling with this word. It never gets there alone.
wakasu.reading_mnemonic: The guide's whole job is making water boil for other people. He jabs a finger at the pot and barks <reading>わかす</reading>, then lights the flame, works the bellows, and refuses to leave until it roars. 'I <reading>walk us</reading> to the boil,' he says. He boils it. The pot never would on its own.
wakasu.description: Japanese has two verbs where English has only 'boil'. This is the transitive side: someone is the subject and puts water, a kettle, or the bath on to boil. If the water just reaches a boil with nobody acting on it, the intransitive verb is the right one.

moeru.meaning_mnemonic: The school groundskeeper is mowing the sports field when the blade clips a stone. One spark drops into the dry cuttings. It catches, and the flame races along the windrow on its own, no one chasing it, no one feeding it. By the time he turns around the whole touchline is burning. The fire just spreads.
moeru.reading_mnemonic: The groundskeeper drops his <reading>mower</reading> and runs for the hose, but the fire is faster than he is. It leaps hedge to hedge across the field while he yells <reading>もえる</reading> at it. The grass is burning and it will not stop. He gives up and watches the touchline glow.
moeru.description: Where English says 'burn' for everything, Japanese uses two verbs. This one is intransitive: whatever is alight is the subject and burns of its own accord. Reach for the separate transitive verb when a person is the one setting something on fire.

moyasu.meaning_mnemonic: Moya and Sue haul a heap of dead branches down to the riverbank. Moya sloshes lamp oil over the pile while Sue gets a match ready. Together they touch it off, then keep feeding the flames so they never drop. Two people, one deliberate fire: that is this word, someone burning something.
moyasu.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Moya, Sue</reading> run the riverbank bonfire every autumn. They rake the fallen leaves, stack them shoulder-high, and set the heap alight on purpose. When a neighbour asks what they are doing, they answer <reading>もやす</reading>. They are burning the whole pile, by their own hand.
moyasu.description: English 'burn' hides a split that Japanese marks with two verbs. This one is transitive: a person, as the subject, burns leaves, trash, or old letters. When something is merely alight and no one is acting on it, the intransitive verb is what you want.

tooru.meaning_mnemonic: The walled path pours everything onto the town's one open road, and all the <kanji>traffic</kanji> lands on it at once. The road has no parking bay, no dead end, no gate. Whatever rolls on at this end rolls off the other end. A truck, three bicycles and a confused goose pass through and are gone.
tooru.reading_mnemonic: At the mountain trail sits a barrier-keeper whose gate snapped off its hinge years back. He still mans the booth. Every hiker, van and stray goat glides past the stump where it stood. He waves each one along, muttering <reading>とおる</reading> — one more <reading>toll</reading> nobody pays, one more thing passing through.
tooru.description: 通る is intransitive: the subject moves through by itself — a car through a tunnel, a road that runs through a town, a voice that carries across a hall. Nothing is being pushed; the thing itself does the passing.

toosu.meaning_mnemonic: One open avenue swallows the whole town's <kanji>traffic</kanji> at its mouth and holds on to none of it. Its entire job is to take what arrives and push it out the far end. A marching band, a runaway shopping cart, one lost tour bus — the avenue threads each one straight through and lets it pass.
toosu.reading_mnemonic: The school caretaker empties the equipment shed through its one high window. Basketballs, a deflated football and somebody's forgotten lunchbox — he gives each one a <reading>toss</reading> up and out. <reading>とおす</reading>, he grunts every time, letting one more object pass through the gap to the field.
toosu.description: 通す is transitive: you take something and put it through — a thread through a needle, a visitor through to the sitting room, a bill through the assembly. What passes is the object; the person or channel doing the passing is the subject.

kooru.meaning_mnemonic: Leave a full water bottle out on the mountain trail one winter night. By dawn the cold has driven all the way into its core. The water is now a bottle-shaped block of ice, hard enough to knock on. To freeze is exactly this: the cold reaches the core and the liquid quits being liquid.
kooru.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank a stubborn swimmer wades in every morning, all winter. One January dawn her toe meets the surface and stops dead. The river has set solid to its <reading>core</reading>. She raps it with a knuckle and sighs: <reading>こおる</reading>. It has frozen clean through, and there is no swim today.
kooru.description: 凍る is only physical freezing — water, ground and pipes turning to ice. It does not carry the English extras: a person frozen with fear, a frozen screen or frozen prices all use different words in Japanese.

tokeru.meaning_mnemonic: Drop a chocolate coin into a hot cup of cocoa and watch the token. Its edges go soft, then round, then gone. The shape blurs out into the brown liquid and you cannot fish it back. To melt or dissolve is that: a solid loses its outline and becomes part of the liquid around it.
tokeru.reading_mnemonic: A boy buys an ice pop at Koichi's konbini and pays with a warm <reading>token</reading> of a coin. He leaves the pop on the sunny sill by the beeping till. Twenty minutes on: a bright puddle with a stick in it. <reading>とける</reading>, sighs Koichi, fetching the mop. It has melted to sticky water.
tokeru.description: This verb has homophones written with other kanji. The 溶ける spelling is the physical one — ice, butter or sugar going liquid. A same-sounding verb written differently means to come untied or to be solved.

shizumu.meaning_mnemonic: Shizu is the one shrine cat who never learned to swim. Set her by the pond and she does not paddle. She drops straight through the water like a stone and settles on the bottom, watching fish go by. Behind the hill the evening sun does the same slow thing: sliding lower, then gone. Heavy things sink, and the sun sets the very same way.
shizumu.reading_mnemonic: Meet Shizu, the shrine cat who never learned to swim. <reading>Shizu zooms</reading> off the mossy step and drops straight to the pond floor, blowing one sad ring of bubbles. When something goes <reading>しずむ</reading>, it does what Shizu does: no paddling, no drifting, just down.

ukabu.meaning_mnemonic: Uka is a very small ghost with no sense of gravity. Let go of her and she does not drop. She rises off your palm and hangs at eye level, turning slowly, saying boo at nobody. Bath water, hot soup, thin air: whatever you rest her on, she comes back up and sits on top of it. To float is her entire personality.
ukabu.reading_mnemonic: Uka the ghost haunts the onigiri shelf at Koichi's konbini. She cannot reach the floor. <reading>Uka boos</reading> and drifts up into the ceiling lights, wobbling over the beeping till like a balloon let go. Picture that for <reading>うかぶ</reading>: rising off whatever should hold you down, then riding light on top.
ukabu.description: Besides physical floating, 浮かぶ is the ordinary word for a thought, a memory, or a name that suddenly surfaces in your mind. English 'float' does not stretch that far, so learn the second sense now: an idea 浮かぶ when it rises into your awareness on its own.

nagareru.meaning_mnemonic: Drop a ribbon into the river and it stops being limp in your hand. The water grabs it and pulls it straight downstream, pointing like an arrow. That steady pull is the <kanji>current</kanji>, and the ribbon only shows what the water was already doing: moving one way, always. When water picks a line and runs down it, that is to <kanji>flow</kanji>.
nagareru.reading_mnemonic: Naga is the kid at the riverbank who begs to rewatch one cartoon every afternoon. <reading>Nag a rerun</reading>, nag a rerun, until the tape rolls itself. The river beside her never needs asking. It keeps moving on its own, downhill, all day. The word for that easy, unstoppable going is <reading>ながれる</reading>.

nagasu.meaning_mnemonic: Sei drags the hose onto the dusty sports field and cranks it open. He does not wait for rain. He aims the nozzle and sends a wide sheet of water across the dirt, steering it with his thumb, pushing leaves off the far edge. He makes the <kanji>current</kanji> himself and decides where it runs, letting the water <kanji>flow</kanji> off the field exactly where he wants it.
nagasu.reading_mnemonic: A goose lives on the school drain and will not move. You <reading>nag a goose</reading> — wave, shout, stamp your boots — and the second it waddles off, you tip the bucket and let the grey puddle pour down the open channel. That deliberate send-off is <reading>ながす</reading>.

kusaru.meaning_mnemonic: Your cousin Sarah brings a casserole to the potluck and forgets to take the leftovers home. The dish sits in her car through a hot weekend. By Monday the top is grey and furry, and the whole car smells like a drain. Anything cousin Sarah leaves in a warm place long enough will rot.
kusaru.reading_mnemonic: Your <reading>cousin Sarah</reading> works the beeping till at Koichi's konbini, and she never checks a date. Give her a week and the egg sandwiches by the door have turned. The bread is green, the filling gone to paste. Koichi lifts one between two fingers, looks at her, and says it flat: 「<reading>くさる</reading>」.

nigeru.meaning_mnemonic: The moment anyone at the dinner table says the word 'dishes', Nigel's chair is empty. His napkin is still settling. Down the hall the front door taps shut, and his tea sits there steaming. Nigel does this at every gathering. First sign of work, and he has run away.
nigeru.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the coach only has to reach for the whistle and <reading>Nigel</reading> is already gone. By the time it blows he is halfway up the back fence of the sports field, blazer flapping. The coach doesn't shout after him anymore. He just writes 「<reading>にげる</reading>」 in the margin by Nigel's name, same as last week.

oikakeru.meaning_mnemonic: A kangaroo hops up to the bus stop, cackling, and lifts the umbrella clean out of your hand. Then it bounds off down the street. You shout 'Oi!' and pound after the roo through every puddle. Running flat out after something to get it back is what it means to chase.
oikakeru.reading_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail you hear a shout behind you. It is the park ranger, yelling <reading>Oi! Cackle-roo!</reading> as she jogs. A monkey has her whole lunch bag. She has been 「<reading>おいかける</reading>」 it since the trailhead, right past the vending machine at the top, and she is not slowing down.
