kotowaru.meaning_mnemonic: Kota stands at the velvet rope like a piece of wall that learned to fold its arms. Your name is not on his list. He doesn't argue and he doesn't soften it. He says one word, points back the way you came, and turns to the next person. Kota at that rope declines every face he doesn't know.
kotowaru.reading_mnemonic: At the festival gate to Grandma Kane's shrine, <reading>Kota</reading> works the rope with his back to the stone <reading>wall</reading>, cats winding round his ankles. A man offers him cash to skip the line. Kota doesn't even look down. Grandma Kane, counting coins by the bell, marks one more in her book: 「<reading>ことわる</reading>」.
kotowaru.description: 断る usually means turning an offer or request down. But it has a second everyday sense: to give notice or ask leave beforehand. The form 断りなく means 'without notice' or 'without permission'. Context tells you which sense applies.

tanomu.meaning_mnemonic: A tan moose the size of a shed lives halfway up the mountain trail. It is the only thing that carries your groceries the last stretch to the vending machine at the top. So every week you climb up, bow to it, and request one more haul. On steep days you rely on it for everything. No moose, no lunch.
tanomu.reading_mnemonic: You need a parcel carried up the mountain trail, so you do what the locals do. You face the big <reading>tan moose</reading> at the trailhead, cup your hands, and call <reading>たのむ</reading>. It chews for a moment, then lumbers off with your parcel. That one word asks it for anything.

tasukaru.meaning_mnemonic: You are stuck to the chest in riverbank mud and cannot pull free. Then <kanji>help</kanji> arrives: one more pair of hands, with all their power thrown behind the pull. You do none of the work. You are just the person on the receiving end, dragged out and left on the grass. That is what it is to be saved.
tasukaru.reading_mnemonic: An old car with two walrus tusks bolted to its bumper waits at the riverbank for this exact moment. You go under; the <reading>tusk car</reading> reverses down the mud, you grab a tusk, and it drags you up. Hold on and you are <reading>たすかる</reading>, dumped safe on the grass.
tasukaru.description: Intransitive: the subject is whoever gets saved or benefits, with no direct object. The near-identical form ending in -eru is the transitive one, used for helping somebody. This word is also a common set phrase meaning that is a big help or what a relief.

tasukeru.meaning_mnemonic: Someone at the school is pinned under a toppled bookshelf. They strain and get nowhere. You run over and become the one more pair of hands, shoving all your power up under the shelf beside theirs. It rises. Putting your hands and your strength in for a person who cannot manage alone is what it means to <kanji>help</kanji>.
tasukeru.reading_mnemonic: A kid at the school wears a bath-towel cape and calls himself <reading>task hero</reading>. Jammed locker, stuck window, a classmate trapped under gym mats: he sprints in and sorts it. To <reading>たすける</reading> is simply to do what that kid does.
tasukeru.description: Transitive: it takes a direct object, the person you help or rescue. The near-identical form ending in -aru is intransitive and means someone gets helped. The vowel before -ru is the whole difference, and the classic mix-up at this level.

shikaru.meaning_mnemonic: A grim grey kangaroo is the house detective at Koichi's konbini. All shift it seeks out tiny crimes: a peeled onigiri wrapper, a shaken fizzy drink, a kid licking the freezer glass. When the seeker corners a culprit, the roo rears up and delivers a loud, finger-wagging lecture. To scold is the whole job.
shikaru.reading_mnemonic: Everyone at Koichi's konbini calls the store detective the <reading>seeker roo</reading>. The grey kangaroo hops the aisles hunting bad behaviour, then stands over the offender and lectures until they say sorry. To <reading>しかる</reading> someone is to give them that full treatment.
shikaru.description: Scolding aimed downward: a parent to a child, a teacher to a student, a boss to a junior. You would not use it with an equal or with anyone above you, so it never means argue with or complain to.

homeru.meaning_mnemonic: A hamster steps up to bat on the school sports field. It swings once and knocks the ball clean over the back fence for a home run. The whole field stands up to praise it, chanting and throwing their caps in the air. One tired little home run, and a stadium's worth of praise poured onto a hamster.
homeru.reading_mnemonic: A kangaroo at the petting zoo has the tidiest pouch you have ever seen. You crouch down and tell her, <reading>home, Roo</reading>, this is a lovely place to live. She sits up, delighted. Say it the Japanese way, <reading>ほめる</reading>, and you have just praised her.

ayamaru.meaning_mnemonic: A llama walks into Koichi's konbini and backs straight into the onigiri shelf by the door. Rice triangles roll across the whole floor. The llama lowers its head, ears flat, plainly full of rue, and bows to Koichi again, and again, and again. A llama drowning in rue at the beeping till is you learning to apologize.
ayamaru.reading_mnemonic: Aya knocks a marble clean through a window at Grandma Kane's shrine. She goes to her ma first and confesses the broken rule. Then she stands in front of Grandma and bows low, sorry, so sorry. <reading>Aya, ma, rule</reading> becomes <reading>あやまる</reading>: to apologize.
ayamaru.description: A separate everyday verb is also read あやまる and means to err or make a mistake; only context, and a different kanji in writing, tell the two apart.

yorokobu.meaning_mnemonic: You haul yourself up the mountain trail to the one vending machine at the top. You press the button with no hope. A cold can thunks into the tray anyway. You are so pleased you hug the machine and tell it, you rock, bub. That rush of gladness over one working machine is what it is to be pleased.
yorokobu.reading_mnemonic: A soggy puppy at the riverbank keeps dropping the same stick at your feet. Every single throw, you tell it, <reading>you rock, bub</reading>. The puppy comes apart with delight, ears flapping, spinning in the mud. That pure, dopey gladness is <reading>よろこぶ</reading>: to be pleased.
yorokobu.description: English 'be pleased' sounds like a passive state, but よろこぶ is an active verb. It describes someone visibly showing delight, most often a person other than the speaker.

okoru-angry.meaning_mnemonic: You take the last pudding out of the fridge. A goose you did not know lived in your kitchen watches from the corner. You ask it, you OK? It is not OK. It rears up with a roar and chases you around the table. Ask a goose if it is okay and get a roar back, that is what it is to get angry.
okoru-angry.reading_mnemonic: Sei opens a dryer at the laundromat and finds a raccoon asleep in the warm drum. It wakes, blinks once, and decides it is furious. She steps back going, <reading>OK, roar</reading>, easy now. Too late, it is already <reading>おこる</reading>, hissing and spitting over its ruined nap. To get angry.
okoru-angry.description: Beyond the inner feeling, おこる is also the everyday word for scolding someone out loud, a parent or teacher おこる at a child. The English 'get angry' misses that active 'tell someone off' sense.

kawakasu.meaning_mnemonic: Kawa the crow holds your soaked paper fan over the coals and turns it fold by fold until every drop is gone. To force the water out of a wet thing on purpose is <vocabulary>to dry</vocabulary> it.
kawakasu.reading_mnemonic: A riverbank crow named Kawa props your soaked fan by the coals and cusses at it until it stiffens. Locals say the fan dried because <reading>Kawa cussed</reading> it, and that kun'yomi, <reading>かわかす</reading>, is <vocabulary>to dry</vocabulary> a wet thing on purpose.

kawaku.meaning_mnemonic: A mountain trail puddle has nobody to bail it out, so it sits in the sun, shrinks to a damp ring, then to nothing. For a thing to lose its water with nobody touching it is <vocabulary>to dry</vocabulary>.
kawaku.reading_mnemonic: The mountain tortoise plods a slow bumper-to-bumper lap of the puddle, a real <reading>car walk</reading>, and by the time it is back the water is gone. No one touched it; the puddle simply did <reading>かわく</reading>, the kun'yomi, and that is <vocabulary>to dry</vocabulary>.
kawaku.description: Written with a different kanji, the same reading also means to be thirsty, from the picture of a throat drying out. Context, not the sound, tells the two apart.

nurasu.meaning_mnemonic: The school nurse finds a nest of rats in the cardboard first-aid bin and drives them out by soaking the cardboard through with a sponge. To put water onto a thing on purpose is <vocabulary>to wet</vocabulary> it.
nurasu.reading_mnemonic: The school nurse deals with the <reading>new rats</reading> in the first-aid bin by wringing a dripping sponge over it until the cardboard sags. She does it on purpose, and that kun'yomi, <reading>ぬらす</reading>, is <vocabulary>to wet</vocabulary> something.

nureru.meaning_mnemonic: A slug crossing the shrine's mossy steps at dawn is soaked through by dew that is just sitting there, nobody pouring a drop. For water to arrive on its own and soak you is <vocabulary>to get wet</vocabulary>.
nureru.reading_mnemonic: The shrine slug hauls itself up the fresh bamboo handrail at dawn and reaches the top glossy and dripping from the dew alone. It went up a <reading>new rail</reading> and came down <reading>ぬれる</reading>, the kun'yomi, so this is <vocabulary>to get wet</vocabulary>.

machigaeru.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>space between</kanji> two pigeonhole dividers is a mail slot, and you shove your letter into the one that <kanji>differs</kanji> from yours by a single room number. Feeding that wrong slot is what it means to <vocabulary>make a mistake</vocabulary>.

shiraseru.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>know</kanji> a fact the moment your arrow thuds into the target. Firing that same fact into someone else's target is <vocabulary>to inform / notify</vocabulary> them.
shiraseru.reading_mnemonic: You already learned 知 is 「し」 back in 知る, so <vocabulary>to inform / notify</vocabulary> someone is just <reading>しらせる</reading>.

mori.meaning_mnemonic: The single character <kanji>forest</kanji> is the entire word, nothing added and nothing dropped. What you met as a kanji and what you say out loud as <vocabulary>forest</vocabulary> are the same thing.
mori.reading_mnemonic: Walk into the <vocabulary>forest</vocabulary> and a mole named <reading>Morrie</reading> shoves his head up between two roots. He insists <reading>もり</reading> is his family name, since he dug every tunnel under these trees.
